newsitem.title: FRANCE: Economists cautious as French markets rally.
newsitem.headline: Economists cautious as French markets rally.

text.p: French bonds and stocks rallied on Wednesday on hopes an EMU-saving compromise was in the works to allow France to ratify a budgetary discipline pact at next week's European Union summit, but some economists urged caution.
"The market really wants to believe France will sign (the stability pact in Amsterdam)," Credit Agricole Indosuez economist Arnaud Mares said. "I think they need to be more cautious."
The German-inspired pact is aimed at policing budgetary discipline after the planned 1999 launch of a single currency.

Stocks and bonds lost ground after the new Socialist government asked on Monday for a delay in signing the pact and said it could not accept the deal agreed by the previous conservative administration unless more stress was put on fighting unemployment.

But the markets got a lift after Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said late Tuesday the French government had told him it did not have to wait to present its policies to the National Assembly on June 19 before ratifying the pact.
The new finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Wednesday that France was seeking a fast resolution of the issue but wanted to "obtain the balance we are seeking".
The Socialists campaigned on a promise to put growth and jobs at the top of the European Union's political agenda.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Germany was ready to agree to a jobs chapter at the Amsterdam summit to be held on June 16 and 17 as long as this did not incur extra EU spending.

The stock market was up 1.3 percent at 2,704.37 in early afternoon, the 10-year bond future was up 32 basis points at 129.80 and the 10-year government bond yield premium over Germany widened to minus eight basis points from minus six.
The franc was slightly softer at 3.3820 per mark on dollar-related weakness, dealers said.

Banque Paribas analyst Dominique Barbet said the EMU picture would be clearer after conservative President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin met Chancellor Helmut Kohl at a regular Franco-German summit on Friday.
"France is demanding much more than a small footnote on growth. It is trying to change the nature of EMU," said Maures.
Another economist said French markets were reluctant to believe the new government would be different from previous ones and actually implement its campaign pledges.

"The market is so used to believing that politicians won't do what they say," he said. He said the new government had a special interest in honouring its pledges after seeing how voters turfed out the centre-right in the recent parliamentary election after it failed to live up to its promises.
"Their political survival is linked to this," he said.
One analyst said the bond market was so awash with cash it was determined to believe in a positive outcome. "All these institutional investors are all very long in cash."
Another analyst at a French bank said there was a danger the French could push Germany, which is insistent that the tough budgetary criteria for launching EMU must not be eased, too far.
"It is clear Kohl wants monetary union. He's clearly wedded to the idea," said Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais.

"But events might take over and the reaction of the German constitional court and the German upper and lower houses to any perceived weakening of the budgetary disciplinary process are unknown factors," he said.
Lukewarm German public support for swapping the mark for the euro heightened the risks, another economist said.
